items.title: One thousand years of historical relics: the Huizhou Documents
items.note: Survey of the discovery, holdings and publication of the Huizhou documents, the largest body of village contracts a signature count could draw on.

items.title: 清代民众识字问题的再认识 (Rethinking popular literacy in the Qing)
items.note: Re-examines Rawski's estimates and argues for studying graded, functional literacies through everyday documents rather than a single rate.

items.title: 签押为证：明清时期画押的源流、类型、文书形态与法律效力 (Signing as proof: hua ya marks in Ming-Qing documents)
items.who: Liu Yonghua 刘永华 and Wen Haibo 温海波
items.note: Typology of the origins, forms and legal force of hua ya marks in contracts, the groundwork any signature-based literacy measure needs.

items.title: Numeracy in early modern Korea, Japan, and China: The age-heaping approach
items.note: Compares age-heaping across the three societies as a proxy for basic numeracy, an indirect human-capital benchmark for Qing literacy estimates.

items.title: 排日账与19世纪徽州乡村社会研究 (Daily account books and nineteenth-century rural Huizhou)
items.note: Uses day-by-day account books kept by Huizhou villagers, direct evidence of practical writing among farming households.

items.title: Daily Life for the Common People of China, 1850 to 1950: Understanding Chaoben Culture
items.note: Studies hand-copied chaoben manuals of letters, contracts and ritual texts, showing what ordinary readers and copyists actually wrote.

items.title: How the Primer-Literate Read Ming Steles: A Digital Speculation
items.note: Introduces the Late Imperial Primer Literacy Sieve, which filters a text to the characters found in primers, to model what basic readers could follow.

items.title: Long Live Keju! The Persistent Effects of China's Civil Examination System
items.who: T. Chen, J. K. Kung and C. Ma
items.note: Links prefecture-level Ming-Qing examination success to modern years of schooling, treating examination density as a proxy for historical human capital.

items.title: Social Order through Contracts: Qingshui River Manuscripts from Southwest China
items.note: First Western-language monograph on the Qingshui River contracts, with a chapter on the scribes and middlemen who wrote them.

items.title: 杂字读物与明清识字问题研究 (Zazi primers and the study of Ming-Qing literacy)
items.note: Proposes using zazi primers, alongside village documents and corpus methods, as direct evidence for the vocabulary of everyday literacy.

items.title: What Meant to Be a Literate in Qing China?
items.note: English statement of the graded-literacy approach, drawing on everyday genres of writing such as account books, primers and contracts.

items.title: “依口代笔”与“依稿代笔”：清代清水江契约的代笔方式 (Dictated and drafted: scribal practice in Qing Qingshui River contracts)
items.note: Shows that contract scribes composed from oral instructions or drafts rather than simply copying, so scribe identity matters for any literacy count.

items.title: The Vernacular World of Pu Songling: Popular Literature and Manuscript Culture in Late Imperial China
items.note: Studies the manuscript copying and adaptation of Pu Songling's vernacular writings, evidence for reading and writing below the examination elite.
